---
title: "Gene Regulation"
description: "How chromatin remodeling complexes find their genomic targets and how their assembly is regulated."
image: featured.jpg
---

Textbook models give the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex one main job:
sliding and evicting nucleosomes to open chromatin so other factors can bind,
with changes in gene expression following changes in accessibility. Our work
keeps finding exceptions. When we perturb SWI/SNF, transcription often changes
even though accessibility does not. This points to a second, scaffolding role,
in which the complex recruits other regulatory proteins independently of its
remodeling activity. We want to know what controls these
accessibility-independent functions, and how the partners SWI/SNF selects
translate into specific patterns of gene expression.

Two regulatory layers appear to tune which partners the complex engages. The
first is post-translational modification of SWI/SNF subunits. Arginine
methylation of the core subunit BAF155, deposited by CARM1, does not change
which version of the complex assembles, but it reshapes the complex's
interactome, especially its contacts with the RNA processing machinery, and
alters nascent transcription without any change in chromatin accessibility. The
second layer is RNA. SWI/SNF and related remodelers bind RNA and act at multiple
steps of the transcription cycle, including polymerase pausing, splicing, and
3′-end processing, and RNA can in turn tune the complex's interactions on a
transcript-specific timescale.

These lines of work frame our mission: to define how SWI/SNF and related
remodelers choose their regulatory partners, and how that choice shapes gene
regulation beyond chromatin accessibility. We combine nascent transcription,
chromatin profiling, and interaction proteomics to connect specific
modifications and RNA contacts to the transcriptional programs they control.
